gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2's measured AC output (1,910 Wh, StorageReview) gives 2.3 charges of a 700 Wh e-bike pack with a 263 Wh margin over the 1,647 Wh two charges need at an 85% charger floor, that the 2.44 kWh StorageReview measured to recharge it means about 1.05 kWh of wall power per bike charge, or that each 2 kWh rival must deliver at least 80–82% of its rated Wh on AC to manage two charges (the Elite 200 V2 measured 92%).
standout_why: PowerStationGearLab, which ChatGPT cited, uses a flat 70% of label capacity it chose itself and works charges for 500, 625, 720, 733 and 840 Wh packs, never 700 Wh. It gives no measured Wh, no cost per charge, no Wh per lb, and a solar refill time only for the Anker C1000 Gen 2. PowerBencher assumes a flat 15% loss, lists no prices and measured nothing. It gives Wh per lb for four units, none of them the Elite 200 V2, S2000 or DELTA 3 Max. Its solar hours are rated input divided into capacity. Our own current page already has the 1,910 Wh measured figure and a 1,800–1,900 Wh two-charge budget. It does not have the charge count with margin, the wall energy per bike charge from the measured 2.44 kWh recharge, the minimum delivery ratio each rival needs, Wh per lb, or $ per charge. Neither ChatGPT answer has a measured figure for any card it showed.
decides: This confirms the Elite 200 V2 ($899) as the only 2 kWh candidate with a third-party measurement that clears two 700 Wh charges (1,910 vs 1,647 Wh needed). It also qualifies ChatGPT's plain-chat pick. On rated figures the Anker SOLIX S2000 is cheaper today ($699.99 on Anker's store) and lighter (56.3 vs 38.8 rated Wh/lb). It still needs at least 81.9% of its 2,010 Wh on AC, which no reviewer has measured, so it is the light, unproven alternative. The DELTA 3 Max ($879, 20.3 kg) is in the same position and needs at least 80.4%. The AC200L is sold out on BLUETTI's US store today, so it should come off the list of live picks. The Elite 300 ($1,199) needs only 54.6% of its rating, so it is the safe-margin pick.

findings.label: Wall-side energy per 700 Wh e-bike charge
findings.value: 824 Wh AC per charge; 1,647 Wh for two
findings.source_title: UL Certified 54.6V 2.5A Ebike Charger For 48V Lithium Battery (VXB)
findings.note: The charger spec reads 'Efficiency: ≥85%' (54.6 V, 2.5 A). 700 ÷ 0.85 = 823.5 Wh; × 2 = 1,647 Wh. This uses the spec's floor, so it is the conservative case.

findings.label: Measured AC output and weight
findings.value: 1,910 Wh discharged of 2,073.6 Wh rated; 53.4 lb (24.2 kg); 2.44 kWh drawn to recharge
findings.source_title: Portable Power Meets Lab-Grade Reliability: BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 Review (StorageReview, 2025-04-25)
findings.note: Quoted: 'The unit discharged 1.91 kWh' and 'it required 2.44kWh'. The review does not state the test load. 1,910 ÷ 2,073.6 = 92.1% of rated.

findings.label: Wall energy per bike charge routed through the station
findings.value: about 1,052 Wh from the outlet per 700 Wh into the bike (78% station round trip)
findings.note: Station round trip: 1,910 ÷ 2,440 = 0.783. Per bike charge: 823.5 ÷ 0.783 = 1,052 Wh.

findings.label: Price and $ per measured Wh / per bike charge
findings.value: $899; $0.47 per measured Wh; $388 per 700 Wh charge of capacity
findings.source_title: BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 Portable Power Station | 2,600W 2,080Wh (BLUETTI US store)

findings.label: Rated and measured Wh per lb

findings.product: BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 + 200 W Solar kit
findings.label: Minimum panel hours to put back one bike charge
findings.value: at least 4.1 h of full 200 W output ($1,199 kit); at least 2.1 h at 400 W ($1,499 2×200 W kit)
findings.source_title: BLUETTI Elite 200 V2+200W Solar (BLUETTI US store)
findings.note: The store lists Elite 200 V2+200W Solar at $1,199 and +2*200W at $1,499 (storecheck). 823.5 ÷ 200 = 4.12 h; 823.5 ÷ 400 = 2.06 h. This lower bound assumes rated panel output and no charge loss. Real hours will be longer.
